analysis.one_liner: Requires the EPA to designate PFAS
analysis.headline: The bill had 30 cosponsors, including two Republicans, but never got a hearing or vote in either House committee before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: PFAS are 'forever chemicals' used in nonstick, waterproof, and stain-resistant products that do not break down and have contaminated drinking water around the country. The bill would have forced the EPA to label the two most notorious PFAS chemicals, PFOA and PFOS, as hazardous substances within 60 days, which makes polluters pay for cleanup, and to set national drinking water limits for several PFAS chemicals. It also would have required toxicity testing of PFAS, limited industrial discharge of the chemicals, banned unsafe incineration of PFAS waste, and sent federal grants to water systems, schools, and territories to find and filter out contamination.
analysis.who_benefits: The tens of millions of Americans whose drinking water, wells, or communities are contaminated with PFAS: the bill sets enforceable drinking water limits, funds filtration for schools and water systems, and shifts cleanup costs onto the companies that made and released the chemicals. People living near PFAS plants or military and industrial sites, and parents of schoolchildren, gain the most.

how_it_helps.text: The EPA would have had to designate PFOA and PFOS as hazardous substances under the Superfund law within 60 days, which makes polluters responsible for paying to clean up contaminated sites.
The EPA would have had to set national drinking water standards for PFOA, PFOS, and at least four other PFAS chemicals within 60 days of enactment.

Community water systems with PFAS in their water would have access to a $500 million per year grant program (fiscal years 2024 through 2028) to pay for treatment technology, prioritizing disadvantaged communities.
Schools and child care programs could get grants for testing drinking water and installing filters, with results required to be made public.
Industrial users in nine priority sectors — including chemical, pulp and paper, textile, metal finishing, and plastics operations — would face enforceable discharge limits for PFAS within four years.
The bill would ban incineration of PFAS waste except at permitted facilities using methods that destroy the chemicals, and would list PFOA and PFOS as hazardous air pollutants.
The EPA would be required to test all PFAS chemicals for toxicity before they can be newly approved for manufacture.

analysis.who_pays: Chemical manufacturers and the many industries that discharge PFAS — the bill's Superfund designation and discharge limits put cleanup and treatment costs on the companies that made and released the chemicals rather than on ratepayers and taxpayers. Water utilities also face monitoring and treatment costs, cushioned by federal grants.

drawbacks.text: The bill bars the EPA from imposing any financial penalties for violating the new PFAS drinking water standards for five years after the rule takes effect, giving water systems a long grace period even where PFAS exceeds health limits.

New PFAS chemicals would be automatically deemed an unreasonable risk and banned from commerce for five years unless exempted, which critics said could block legitimate uses such as some medical devices, components, and specialized industrial applications.

The mandates fall on water utilities and municipal treatment plants as well as polluters; where the $500 million per year in grants falls short, the cost of filtering PFAS can be passed to households through water rates.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health benefit is large and the design is broadly sensible: it puts cleanup and discharge costs on the industries that released the chemicals and sends targeted grants to schools, disadvantaged water systems, and territories. The main honest concerns are the five-year enforcement moratorium on drinking water penalties and the possibility that water rates rise in places the grants do not fully cover. On balance the costs fall mostly on the companies that profited from the chemicals.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to two House committees on the day it was introduced, then passed down to subcommittees, and no committee ever acted on it before the Congress ended, so it never came to a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Debbie Dingell introduced the PFAS Action Act of 2023 on December 14, 2023, with 15 original cosponsors including Republican Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick.
The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Transportation and Infrastructure Committees the day it was introduced.
In the following weeks it was referred to the Subcommittee on Environment, Manufacturing, and Critical Materials and the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment.
No further action was taken — no hearing, markup, or vote — and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill.
The bill attracted 30 cosponsors, 28 Democrats and 2 Republicans.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PFAS manufacturers and the industrial sectors that would have faced Superfund cleanup liability, discharge limits, and toxicity testing requirements are better off because the bill never advanced; households with contaminated water gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Debbie Dingell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and organized 15 original cosponsors.

for.name: Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick
for.what_they_did: One of two Republicans among the bill's original cosponsors, giving it a bipartisan edge.

for.name: 30 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support but the bill never reached the floor for a vote.

against.name: Rep. Cathy McMorris Rodgers

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup of the bill, which held primary jurisdiction over most of its provisions.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was heavily Democratic — 28 of 30 — with two Republicans, and the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists; a prior version of the same bill had passed the House in the previous Congress.

industries.note: The bill would make PFOA and PFOS Superfund hazardous substances within 60 days, forcing makers and users to pay for cleanup of contaminated sites, and would require toxicity testing of all PFAS. Companies that manufactured these chemicals have faced massive liability for the contamination.

industries.industry: Industrial PFAS dischargers (chemicals, pulp and paper, textiles, metal finishing, plastics, leather, paint, electronics)
industries.note: Nine priority industries would face enforceable federal discharge limits for PFAS within four years and must notify treatment plants before releasing PFAS. Their costs are the public's protection.

industries.industry: Water utilities and publicly owned treatment works
industries.note: Utilities gain $500 million per year in treatment grants and $200 million per year for treatment plants, but must monitor and treat PFAS and face the new standards — with a five-year shield from penalties written into the bill. Costs can eventually reach households through rates.

Mandated drinking water monitoring, school testing grants, and a $100 million per year school filtration program create demand for testing laboratories and filtration equipment. Households get cleaner water alongside the industry's gain.
PFAS waste could only be incinerated at permitted facilities using methods that destroy the chemicals, with violations treated as hazardous waste infractions carrying penalties.

industries.industry: Consumer product makers (cookware, carpet, clothing, food packaging)
industries.note: A voluntary PFAS-free label would let manufacturers signal safer products to consumers; any companies reformulating away from PFAS face costs, and shoppers get clearer information.
